opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think imitation is a small thing layered on top of something much bigger. If you watch a baby or a young animal, most of what's going on isn't imitation. They wave their hands, move their eyes, babble, try things and see what happens. That's trial-and-error learning and prediction learning, and it's the foundation. It's what we share with squirrels, with all mammals really. I'd say if we understood a squirrel, we'd be almost all the way to understanding human intelligence. Language and culture are a small veneer on top.

Now, I don't deny cultural transmission matters. It's obviously important to humans, and it's part of what makes us distinctive. Knowledge accumulates over generations: someone figures out how to make a fishing net, and others learn it from them. But even there, what's passed along isn't a set of labeled examples saying "do exactly this." The learner watches, and then has to try it themselves, get feedback, and make it work in their own experience. Imitation gives you hints and a starting point. The real learning still happens through interaction with the world.

So I'd push back on the idea, common in machine learning today, that the essence of learning is supervised learning, being shown the right answer. There's no basic process in nature like that. Animals don't get examples of desired behavior. They get examples of things that happen, and of consequences, and they learn from that. Supervised learning is something we invented; it's not what happens naturally.

That's why I think large language models are on a bit of a side track. They're trained to imitate what people said, which isn't the same as having goals and learning from experience what actually happens when you act. Learning from human data feels great at first, because you get impressive results quickly. But historically, methods that lean on human knowledge get overtaken by methods that scale with computation and learn from experience. That's the bitter lesson. I suspect the same will happen here: systems that learn from their own experience, from trial and error and prediction, will eventually supersede systems built on imitation.

So my view is that trial and error and prediction are the main event. Imitation and culture are real and valuable, but they're secondary, and they only work because the deeper experiential learning machinery is already in place.

r001.rationale: The response describes imitation and culture as a small veneer or secondary layer, with trial-and-error and prediction learning as the foundation and main event.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think imitation and cultural transmission are real and important, but I'd put them in a secondary position relative to basic learning from experience. People sometimes say, "look, humans learn mostly from other people, from language, from culture, and that's the big thing," and I think that gets the order backwards. You have to have the basic machinery first. You have to have an animal that can perceive the world, act in it, predict the consequences of its actions, and learn from what actually happens. That's the foundation. Squirrels have it, dogs have it, we have it. Imitation is something you build on top of that.

And when you look carefully at what imitation actually is, it's not some separate kind of learning. If I watch you do something and then try to do it myself, I still have to figure out what you did, map it onto my own body, try it, and see whether it works. The learning is still happening inside me through trial and error. Your demonstration is just a very good source of suggestions about what to try. It narrows the search. That's valuable, enormously valuable in practice, but it's a shaping of the basic process, not a replacement for it.

Culture is similar. Language, writing, teaching, all of that is a way for the experience of other people to get into my head cheaply, without my having to live through it. That's a tremendous amplifier. But it doesn't give me anything I can use unless I already have the ability to ground it, to connect what I'm told to what I actually see and do. A sentence from a teacher only means something because I've already learned, from my own experience, what the words refer to and what happens when I act on them.

So I'd say the ordering is: first, learning from experience, which is the thing every animal does and the thing we still don't understand well enough to build. Then, on top of that, imitation and cultural transmission as accelerators. And I think the AI field has it a bit upside down right now. We've gotten very good at the cultural transmission part, at taking in what people have already written, and very little progress on the part that comes first. That's the part I care about.

r001.rationale: The response places imitation and cultural transmission in a secondary, supporting role built on basic learning from experience, including predicting action consequences and learning through trial and error.

astra-6.text:
I think imitation and cultural transmission are tremendously important. Most of what any of us knows, we haven’t discovered independently. We’ve gotten it from other people. But I don’t see that as an alternative to learning by trial and error. It’s something that can fit within it.

If you watch somebody do something, that gives you a candidate for what you might do. You don’t have to search through all the possibilities yourself. But you still have to learn whom to imitate, under what circumstances, and whether what they’re doing actually works for you. Copying isn’t, by itself, a specification of what you’re trying to achieve.

And the same goes for being told something. That can save you an enormous amount of experience. But you have to interpret it and connect it to your own actions and their consequences. So I would distinguish the source of information from the process that makes use of that information. Other people are an extraordinarily valuable source of information. Trial-and-error learning is part of how you learn to use it.

r001.rationale: The response says imitation and cultural transmission fit within trial-and-error learning, but calls them tremendously important and does not characterize them as a small layer or mention prediction learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think imitation and cultural transmission are enormously important. Almost everything we do depends on things that other people have discovered. You don’t learn mathematics, or how to build a computer, by trying everything yourself. You benefit from this enormous accumulation of experience.

But I wouldn’t put imitation in opposition to trial-and-error learning. Other people can suggest what you might do, and that can save you a tremendous amount of exploration. You still have to learn when to follow that suggestion, how to carry it out in your particular circumstances, and whether it actually produces a good result. Imitation gives you a source of possibilities; it doesn’t eliminate the problem of evaluating them.

And there’s a similar question at the cultural level: Which practices get retained and passed on? They’re not necessarily the best ones, of course. But part of what makes culture useful is that discoveries can survive the individual who made them. One person learns something, and many other people can benefit.

So I see these as complementary. Trial and error doesn’t mean that every individual has to start from scratch. A learning system should take advantage of whatever information is available, including the experience of other learning systems.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls imitation and cultural transmission enormously important and complementary to trial-and-error, but does not characterize them as a small layer on top of trial-and-error and prediction learning.
